lines.text: set every trace $E(s) = 0$; set $S$ to the start state
take the action $\pi$ gives for $S$; see $R$ and $S'$
for every state $s$: $V(s) \leftarrow V(s) + \alpha\delta E(s)$, then $E(s) \leftarrow \gamma\lambda E(s)$

verification.note: Pseudocode compared with the text layer of Figure 7.7; the implementation is checked by ch07.offline-equivalence, ch07.true-online-mc and ch07.fig7-6.

explainer.problem: Combine the one-step TD error with a short memory of recently visited states, so that each error updates many earlier states at once, approximating the λ-return algorithm causally and incrementally.

derivation.why: Off-line (V fixed), the λ-return error is a discounted sum of later TD errors.
Swap the order of summation: the inner sum is the accumulating trace, so off-line TD(λ) makes the λ-return algorithm's updates exactly.

example.text: With γ = 1 and λ = 0.8, a state visited at time 0 and again at time 2 has accumulating trace $0.8^2 + 1 = 1.64$ at time 2 (replacing: 1; dutch with α = 0.5: $0.5 \cdot 0.64 + 1 = 1.32$). A TD error of 0.5 with α = 0.1 then raises a state whose trace is 0.64 by $0.1 \cdot 0.5 \cdot 0.64 = 0.032$.

advantages: Causal and incremental: needs only the current TD error and the traces.
λ moves smoothly from TD(0) to Monte Carlo; intermediate λ is usually best (Figure 7.6).
Off-line it equals the λ-return algorithm exactly.
limitations: On-line with accumulating traces it can be unstable for large α and λ (Figure 7.6).
Updating every state every step is costly unless near-zero traces are skipped (§7.8).

comparisons.point: TD(0) is the case λ = 0: only the state just left is updated.
True on-line TD(λ) adds correction terms that make it match a real-time λ-return algorithm exactly.

lines.text: set every trace $E(s) = 0$; set $S$ to the start state
take the action $\pi$ gives for $S$; see $R$ and $S'$
for every state $s$: $V(s) \leftarrow V(s) + \alpha(\delta + \Delta)E(s)$, then $E(s) \leftarrow \gamma\lambda E(s)$

verification.note: Pseudocode compared with the text layer of Figure 7.10; check ch07.true-online-mc confirms its λ = 1 equivalence with constant-α MC.

explainer.problem: Get an on-line, causal algorithm whose values match a forward-view (λ-return) algorithm exactly at every step, not just approximately.

derivation.why: The draft's update (p. 182): TD(λ) with dutch traces plus two terms correcting for the change in $V(S_t)$ since it was last used as a target.

example.text: With λ = 1, after each episode its values equal those of constant-α MC applied at the episode's end in time order, to rounding error, even though it updated on-line (check ch07.true-online-mc).

advantages: Exactly equivalent to a real-time λ-return algorithm (van Seijen and Sutton, 2014).
Robust to α and λ on the 19-state walk, like dutch traces.
limitations: Slightly more computation per step than TD(λ).
On the 19-state walk it is not clearly better than TD(λ) with dutch traces (p. 182).

comparisons.point: TD(λ) with dutch traces, minus the correction terms.

lines.text: set every trace $E(s, a) = 0$; choose $S$ and $A$
choose $A'$ from $S'$ with the policy derived from $Q$ (e.g. ε-greedy)
raise $E(S, A)$: accumulating, dutch or replacing, as in TD(λ)
for every pair: $Q(s, a) \leftarrow Q(s, a) + \alpha\delta E(s, a)$, then $E(s, a) \leftarrow \gamma\lambda E(s, a)$

verification.note: Pseudocode compared with the text layer of Figure 7.12; Example 7.2 is reproduced by check ch07.traces-gridworld.

explainer.problem: On-policy control that passes each TD error back to many recent state–action pairs, so that a reward found at the end of a long path improves the whole path at once.

example.text: Example 7.2: one episode ends in the only reward after 20 moves, from $Q = 0$ with α = 0.1. One-step Sarsa raises one action value (the last, by 0.1). Sarsa(λ) with λ = 0.9 raises all 20, by $0.1 \cdot 0.9^k$ for the move k steps before the end: 0.0729 three steps back.

advantages: Much faster credit assignment over long paths (Example 7.2).
On-policy, like Sarsa, so the ε-greedy behaviour is taken into account.
limitations: More computation per step than one-step Sarsa.
No convergence proof for control with 0 < λ < 1 (bibliographical remarks, p. 192).

comparisons.point: One-step Sarsa is the case λ = 0.
Watkins's Q(λ) uses the max in δ and cuts the traces after exploratory actions.

lines.text: set every trace $E(s, a) = 0$; choose $S$ and $A$
choose $A'$ from $S'$ with the policy derived from $Q$ (e.g. ε-greedy)
$A^* \leftarrow \arg\max_a Q(S', a)$, choosing $A'$ itself when it is among the best
for every pair: $Q(s, a) \leftarrow Q(s, a) + \alpha\delta E(s, a)$; then $E(s, a) \leftarrow \gamma\lambda E(s, a)$ if $A' = A^*$, else $E(s, a) \leftarrow 0$

verification.note: Pseudocode compared with the text layer of Figure 7.15; check ch07.watkins confirms λ = 0 is Q-learning and that traces are cut exactly after nongreedy actions.

explainer.problem: Add eligibility traces to off-policy Q-learning without crediting earlier actions with experience gathered after the agent stopped following the greedy policy.

example.text: In the Example 7.2 path, declare move 15 exploratory: the traces are cut as it is chosen, so when the reward arrives only moves 15–20 are credited; the first 14 get nothing (lab panel 'Credit from one episode').

advantages: Off-policy: learns about the greedy policy while exploring.
With λ = 0 it is one-step Q-learning (check ch07.watkins).
limitations: Exploratory actions cut the traces, so with frequent exploration it is little faster than Q-learning.
Treats off-policy deviation as all or nothing and bootstraps at every deviation, even with λ = 1 (§7.7).

comparisons.point: Sarsa(λ) never cuts its traces, since it learns about the policy it follows.
